Do You Need an Attorney for Probate in Texas?

You do not need an attorney for every situation involving a deceased person’s property in Texas. However, most formal probate cases require legal representation because the executor or administrator is acting on behalf of the estate and other interested parties—not only themselves.

In Harris County and many other Texas counties, a person seeking appointment as executor or administrator generally must be represented by a licensed probate attorney. Limited alternatives may be available when the estate is small, probate administration is unnecessary, or the applicant is the only beneficiary.

Whether you need an attorney depends on the assets, debts, will, beneficiaries, family relationships, and type of probate procedure involved.

Is a Probate Attorney Required in Texas?

A Texas statute does not simply say that every probate applicant must hire an attorney.

However, Texas law generally prohibits a person who is not a licensed lawyer from representing other individuals or legal interests in court.

An executor or administrator usually represents more than their own personal interests. They may be responsible for:

  • The estate
  • Beneficiaries
  • Heirs
  • Creditors
  • Other interested parties

Because of this, many Texas probate courts require applicants seeking formal appointment as personal representative to have an attorney.

Why Can’t an Executor Usually Handle Probate Alone?

An executor is not simply appearing in court for themselves.

Once appointed, the executor becomes a fiduciary responsible for administering property that may belong to several beneficiaries and may be subject to creditor claims.

The executor may need to:

  • File the will with the probate court
  • Request Letters Testamentary
  • Notify beneficiaries
  • Identify and protect estate assets
  • Address creditor claims
  • Prepare an inventory or affidavit in lieu of inventory
  • Handle estate expenses
  • Transfer or sell property
  • Distribute remaining assets

Preparing legal pleadings and representing the estate in court can be considered the practice of law. A non-lawyer generally cannot provide that representation for the estate or other beneficiaries.

What Is the Difference Between Filing Probate and Representing Yourself?

A person generally has the right to represent their own individual interests in court. This is called appearing pro se.

The problem in probate is that an applicant is often not representing only themselves.

For example, a daughter named executor in her father’s will may also be responsible for protecting property that will be distributed to her siblings. She may also need to respond to claims made by creditors.

In that situation, she is acting for the estate and other people. That usually requires a licensed attorney.

When Might You Handle a Texas Estate Without an Attorney?

Limited procedures may sometimes be completed without a lawyer.

Possible examples include:

  • Certain small estate affidavits
  • Collecting assets that pass directly by beneficiary designation
  • Using a transfer-on-death designation
  • Receiving life insurance proceeds as a named beneficiary
  • Accessing payable-on-death accounts
  • Transferring certain jointly owned property
  • Very limited probate proceedings involving a sole beneficiary

Even when an attorney is not legally required, legal advice may help determine whether the procedure is appropriate.

Can You File a Small Estate Affidavit Without an Attorney?

In many Texas counties, heirs may be able to prepare and file a Small Estate Affidavit without hiring an attorney.

A Small Estate Affidavit is a simplified procedure available only when specific legal requirements are satisfied.

Among other requirements, the deceased person generally must have died without a will, and the value of qualifying probate assets must fall within the statutory limit after excluding homestead and exempt property.

A Small Estate Affidavit may not be appropriate when:

  • The deceased left a valid will
  • The estate exceeds the applicable asset limit
  • There are significant creditor disputes
  • The heirs cannot agree
  • The estate owns complicated business interests
  • The affidavit cannot effectively transfer the property involved

Using the wrong procedure can create delays and additional expense.

Can You Probate a Will as a Muniment of Title Without a Lawyer?

A muniment of title is a Texas probate procedure that may transfer property under a valid will without appointing an executor to administer the estate.

It may be available when:

  • There is a valid will
  • There is no need for estate administration
  • The estate has no unpaid debts other than certain debts secured by real estate

Some courts may permit a person to proceed without an attorney when the applicant is the executor and only beneficiary and is truly representing only their own interests.

However, court policies differ, and preparing the application, proving the will, and obtaining the proper order still involve legal requirements.

What If You Are the Only Beneficiary?

Being the only beneficiary may create a limited exception to the usual requirement for an attorney.

Texas courts have recognized that an executor who is also the sole beneficiary may sometimes represent themselves because no other beneficiary’s interest is involved.

That does not mean every sole-beneficiary case can proceed without counsel.

Other issues may still require an attorney, including:

  • Creditor claims
  • Disputed ownership
  • Will contests
  • Tax issues
  • Title problems
  • Complex estate assets

The probate court’s local rules and policies also matter.

Does Harris County Require a Probate Attorney?

Harris County Probate Courts generally require applicants seeking Letters Testamentary, Letters of Administration, determinations of heirship, or guardianship appointments to be represented by a licensed attorney.

This is especially relevant to Houston families because probate matters involving Houston residents are commonly filed in Harris County.

The requirement exists because the applicant is normally representing the estate and the interests of third parties.

What Does a Texas Probate Attorney Do?

A probate attorney guides the executor, administrator, beneficiaries, or heirs through the court process.

Common services include:

  • Determining whether probate is necessary
  • Identifying the appropriate probate procedure
  • Preparing and filing the application
  • Scheduling and attending the probate hearing
  • Helping the executor qualify
  • Obtaining Letters Testamentary or Letters of Administration
  • Providing required notices
  • Addressing creditor claims
  • Preparing inventories and related filings
  • Transferring estate assets
  • Advising the executor about fiduciary duties
  • Helping close or complete the estate

The lawyer generally represents the executor or administrator in their fiduciary capacity rather than representing every beneficiary individually.

Does Having a Will Eliminate the Need for a Probate Attorney?

No. A will can make probate easier, but it does not automatically eliminate probate or the need for legal representation.

The will may identify:

  • The beneficiaries
  • The executor
  • How property should be distributed
  • Whether independent administration is authorized
  • Whether the executor may serve without bond

However, the probate court must generally admit the will before the executor receives authority to act.

The person named as executor does not automatically receive legal control over estate assets at the moment of death.

What Is Independent Administration?

Independent administration allows an executor or administrator to handle many estate matters without repeatedly asking the probate court for approval.

Texas is known for allowing relatively streamlined independent administrations when the will authorizes them or all qualified distributees agree.

An independent executor may often:

  • Pay valid estate expenses
  • Manage estate assets
  • Sell certain property
  • Settle claims
  • Distribute property

Independent administration reduces court supervision, but it does not eliminate fiduciary duties or the usual need for an attorney at the beginning of the case.

What Happens If There Is No Will?

When someone dies without a valid will, they are considered to have died intestate.

Texas intestacy law determines who inherits the property.

A probate court may need to:

  • Determine the legal heirs
  • Appoint an administrator
  • Approve a dependent or independent administration
  • Address creditor claims
  • Authorize property transfers

Probate without a will is often more complicated because the family cannot rely on written instructions naming an executor or explaining how assets should be divided.

Do You Need an Attorney for a Determination of Heirship?

Generally, yes.

A determination of heirship is a court proceeding used to identify the legal heirs of someone who died without a valid will or whose will did not dispose of all property.

The case may require:

  • An application
  • Notice to interested parties
  • Appointment of an attorney ad litem
  • Testimony from disinterested witnesses
  • A court hearing
  • A final judgment identifying the heirs

Because multiple heirs and legal interests are involved, a licensed probate attorney is normally required.

When Is Hiring a Probate Attorney Especially Important?

Legal representation is particularly important when:

  • Beneficiaries disagree
  • Someone contests the will
  • The estate has substantial debt
  • The estate owns real estate in multiple counties
  • The deceased owned a business
  • Property ownership is unclear
  • An heir cannot be located
  • A beneficiary is a minor
  • The executor is accused of misconduct
  • There are tax concerns
  • The original will is missing
  • The will is handwritten or improperly executed

These issues can turn a routine probate matter into contested litigation.

Can the Estate Pay the Probate Attorney’s Fees?

Reasonable and necessary attorney’s fees related to estate administration may often be paid from estate assets.

This means the executor may not always need to pay the entire legal fee personally.

Whether the estate can pay a specific expense depends on:

  • The work performed
  • Whether the services benefited the estate
  • The terms of the will
  • The estate’s available assets
  • Applicable Texas law

Fees generated by an executor’s personal misconduct or individual dispute may receive different treatment.

How Much Does a Probate Attorney Cost in Texas?

There is no single price for every Texas probate case.

Cost may depend on:

  • The type of probate procedure
  • The size and complexity of the estate
  • Whether the matter is contested
  • The number of beneficiaries and creditors
  • The type of property involved
  • The county where probate is filed
  • The amount of work required

A straightforward independent administration with a valid will usually costs less than a contested heirship case or will dispute.

Can Probate Be Avoided Entirely?

Sometimes, not every estate requires formal probate.

Assets may pass outside probate through:

  • Life insurance beneficiary designations
  • Retirement account beneficiaries
  • Payable-on-death bank accounts
  • Transfer-on-death investment accounts
  • Joint ownership with right of survivorship
  • Transfer-on-death deeds
  • Lady Bird deeds
  • Revocable living trusts

If all significant assets pass through non-probate arrangements, a court administration may not be necessary.

However, families should confirm how each asset is titled before assuming probate can be avoided.

What Are the Risks of Trying to Handle Probate Without a Lawyer?

Probate mistakes may create:

  • Rejected court filings
  • Missed deadlines
  • Invalid notices
  • Creditor disputes
  • Title problems
  • Improper distributions
  • Personal liability for the executor
  • Family conflict
  • Additional court costs

An executor who distributes assets too early or fails to address valid estate obligations may be held responsible for resulting losses.

How Do You Know Which Probate Procedure to Use?

The correct procedure depends on the estate’s facts.

Possible Texas procedures include:

  • Independent administration
  • Dependent administration
  • Probate of a will as a muniment of title
  • Small Estate Affidavit
  • Determination of heirship
  • Affidavit of heirship for certain real estate matters
  • Family allowance or exempt-property proceedings

Choosing the wrong procedure can cause the court to reject the application or may fail to transfer the property effectively.

How The Lange Firm Helps Houston and Texas Families

The Lange Firm helps families in Houston and throughout Texas with probate and estate administration matters involving:

  • Probating wills
  • Independent administration
  • Executor representation
  • Determinations of heirship
  • Small estate options
  • Muniment of title proceedings
  • Real estate transfers after death
  • Creditor and beneficiary issues
  • Probate disputes

Determining whether an attorney is required begins with identifying the assets, debts, beneficiaries, and legal procedure appropriate for the estate.

Frequently Asked Questions About Probate Attorneys in Texas

Do you legally need an attorney for probate in Texas?

Most formal probate applicants seeking appointment as executor or administrator need an attorney because they are representing the estate and the interests of other parties. Limited exceptions may apply.

Can an executor represent themselves in Texas probate court?

Usually not when the executor is representing an estate with multiple beneficiaries or creditors. An executor who is also the sole beneficiary may sometimes qualify for a limited exception.

Can I file a Small Estate Affidavit without an attorney?

Many Texas counties permit heirs to file a qualifying Small Estate Affidavit without an attorney, but the estate must satisfy strict statutory requirements.

Does a will mean probate is unnecessary?

No. A will provides instructions for distributing property, but it often must be admitted to probate before the executor receives legal authority.

Can the estate pay the probate lawyer?

Reasonable and necessary attorney’s fees related to administering the estate may often be paid from estate assets, depending on the circumstances.

Conclusion

You do not need a probate attorney for every asset transfer after a death. However, most formal Texas probate administrations require an attorney because the executor or administrator represents the estate and other interested parties.

  • Formal applications for Letters Testamentary or Letters of Administration usually require legal representation.
  • Limited alternatives may include qualifying Small Estate Affidavits and certain sole-beneficiary proceedings.
  • A probate attorney can help select the correct procedure, satisfy court requirements, and protect the executor from costly mistakes.

The best first step is determining whether formal probate is required at all and, if so, which Texas procedure fits the estate.

  • Texas Estates Code Chapter 304: Personal Representatives
  • Bexar County Probate Court: Pro Se Applicant Policy
